measures.methodNote: Hospital-level relative price for inpatient and outpatient services, 2020-2022, from RAND annex Table 1; 74 of 86 Kentucky hospitals have a value. Headline is the unweighted median across those hospitals.
measures.methodology: RAND re-prices private (employer-sponsored) claims with Medicare's own payment formulas for the same hospital and service, then divides what the plan and patient paid by what Medicare would have paid. Its claims come from self-insured employers, participating health plans and 12 state all-payer claims databases (Kentucky's is not one of them), so it covers a sample of commercially insured people, not every plan. Hospital prices are case-mix adjusted and include facility and related professional claims; a blank hospital value means fewer than 11 claims. Data are 2020-2022, published December 2024. Small hospitals often rest on a few hundred claims, so their figures are less stable; the number of stays and services is shown with each hospital. The system named in each row is RAND's attribution from the AHRQ Compendium of U.S. Health Systems for that period and can differ from current CMS ownership.

measures.methodNote: Payment level as % of Medicare = (payment level as % of average commercial rate, HRIP CY 2026 preprint Table 2) x (Kentucky commercial facility price as % of Medicare, RAND Round 5.1, 2022: inpatient 232.8%, outpatient 268.4%).
measures.methodology: This converts Kentucky's directed-payment levels, which the CMS preprint states as a percent of the average commercial rate, into an approximate percent of Medicare so they can sit beside Indiana's testimony. The two inputs measure different things: Kentucky's commercial rate is the average payment per day (inpatient) or payment-to-charge ratio (outpatient) from the top five commercial payers at eligible hospitals, while RAND's ratio is case-mix adjusted from a sample of employer claims in 2020-2022. Medicaid patients also use a different mix of services. Treat the result as an order of magnitude, not a rate.

measures.methodNote: Commercial dollars per inpatient case = RAND Round 5.1 relative price for inpatient facility services (2020-2022) x the same hospital's Medicare inpatient payment per discharge. Medicare payment per discharge = (Worksheet E Part A lines 1.01 + 1.02 MS-DRG operating payments + line 2 outliers + line 29 IME + line 34 DSH) / Worksheet S-3 Part I line 14 column 13 Title XVIII discharges, from the CMS 2024 Hospital Provider Cost Report file (2023 file where the 2024 report is missing, under 180 days, or incomplete: line 1.01 or 1.02 blank for a report spanning October 1, or under $3,000 per discharge). Matched on Medicare provider number (CCN): 50 of 51 Kentucky hospitals with a RAND inpatient facility price have a usable cost report; 86 RAND hospitals in all. Headline is the unweighted median of matched hospitals. Outpatient rows keep the RAND posting but have no dollar value (see reason).
measures.methodology: RAND reports each hospital's commercial price as a percent of what Medicare would have paid that same hospital, using Medicare's own formulas, which already adjust for case mix, wages, teaching (IME) and disproportionate share (DSH). To turn that percent into dollars, it is multiplied by what Medicare actually paid the hospital per traditional-Medicare inpatient discharge in its own cost report; the result reads as "what commercial plans pay for a stay like the hospital's average Medicare stay", facility payments only.RAND covers 2020-2022 claims and the cost reports cover fiscal years ending 2024-2025, so the method assumes each hospital's commercial-to-Medicare ratio held into 2024; dollars are therefore approximate 2024 dollars. Medicare patients are older and sicker than commercial patients, so a typical commercial stay costs less than these figures; RAND's own case-mix-standardized commercial price per stay is shown beside each row for comparison. Critical access hospitals are paid on cost and their Medicare payments are not in the public file, and the cost report has no count of outpatient services, so those rows carry the percent but no dollar figure.

measures.bundleDefinition: Inpatient rows: facility only, excludes professional fees. Commercial side = RAND's inpatient facility relative price (private allowed amount on facility claims, plan plus patient share, divided by Medicare's simulated facility payment for the same stays). Medicare side = MS-DRG operating payment (with wage-index adjustment) plus outliers, IME and DSH per traditional-Medicare discharge. Not included on either side: physician and other professional fees, Medicare capital and pass-through payments (graduate medical education, organ acquisition, bad debt), uncompensated-care payments (RAND includes a scaled version; the public file does not carry them), post-discharge care, and non-claims payments such as quality bonuses. Outpatient rows: facility payment per separately payable OPPS service line, facility only, excludes professional fees.

measures.methodology: Kentucky's HRIP preprint states payment levels as a percent of the average commercial rate, but it also publishes dollar amounts: a uniform add-on per inpatient discharge and the year's total HRIP payments for inpatient and outpatient care. Dividing the dollar add-on by its percent gives the average commercial rate per discharge the state used, and every other percent converts from that. These are statewide averages across all HRIP-eligible hospitals (university and state mental hospitals excluded), for managed-care members only, facility payments only. The preprint has no per-hospital amounts and no count of outpatient visits, so outpatient figures are annual totals, not per visit. The commercial rate is the state's own measure (top five commercial payers' payment per day, inpatient) and the Medicare-equivalent row is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

notes:
SCOPE AND YEARS. Hospitals = Kentucky CCNs with HCRIS facility type STH (short-term acute) or CAH in CMS's 2024 Hospital Provider Cost Report file (cost reports beginning in 2024; reports of 180+ days end between 2024-09 and 2025-08), reposted by CMS 2026-10-05: 90 hospitals (29 critical access, 41 rural non-CAH, 20 urban). Four CCNs that filed for 2023 have no 2024 report (180106 Medical Center of Albany, a name that appears in 2024 as CAH 181333; 180154 Pineville Community Health Center; 180155 and 180156 ARH Advanced Care, long-term care). Cost reports under 180 days (180095 Crittenden pre-change of ownership, 180139 Kentucky River Medical Center) are in rows but excluded from medians and thirds. Ownership: CMS Hospital All Owners and Enrollments, 2026-09-29 snapshot. Schedule H: latest Form 990 per EIN in the IRS TEOS e-file indexes for 2025 and 2026 (tax years ending 2024-06 to 2025-10; one filer 2023-06). RAND: Round 5.1 (2020-2022 data; state figures 2022), published Dec 2024. HRIP: CMS-approved preprints for CY 2024 and CY 2026.

DEFINITIONS. Operating margin = G-3 net income from service to patients / net patient revenue. Total margin = net income / (net patient revenue + other income), the SME view's definition. Thirds use 10% and 0% cut points: double-digit, low single-digit (0 to under 10%), negative. On operating margin Kentucky splits about 30% / 33% / 38% (26 / 29 / 33 of 88 hospitals); on total margin the split is about 63% / 30% / 8%, because many hospitals book large amounts as other income (for some, possibly directed payments, grants or investment income; the cost report does not say which). Show both and describe, do not rank. Keep critical access, rural and urban hospitals in separate rows (Indiana's "surgical, not blunt" approach and the co-chair's rural question at 0:12:18).

ORGANIZATION-ONLY RULE. System labels come only from organizational owners (TYPE - OWNER = O) and enrolling organizations in CMS files; individual owner rows are never read into the output, and every label passes the ChainLabelAtoms.ResolveChainLabel organization-marker allowlist (ported verbatim); a failing label would show as 'CMS associate <id> (label withheld)'. No label was withheld in this build. 'No multi-hospital parent reported to CMS' is not the same as independent: nonprofit parents often do not appear in PECOS, so hospital rows also carry systemPerAhrqViaRand, RAND's 2020-2022 AHRQ Compendium attribution. The two can disagree because of acquisitions and management contracts since 2022. Every figure is descriptive; low or negative margins and low cash are facts for review, not findings about any hospital.

INDIANA TESTIMONY (Indiana Secretary of Health and Family Services, subcommittee meeting 2026-10-28; not data). About a third of Indiana hospitals have double-digit margins, a third low single digits, a third negative (0:09:54-0:10:39). The largest systems hold over $2 billion in cash and investments (0:10:52). Indiana's directed payments are 124%-158% of Medicare, tiered, highest for critical access and rural (0:14:37-0:15:20). Commercial prices are over 300% of Medicare (0:09:30). TiC files matched claims for 21% of prices (0:41:36). Use these as quoted testimony with timestamps, never as benchmarks.

FEASIBILITY NOTE FOR THE MEMBER WHO ASKED FOR A COMMERCIAL-PAYER COMPARISON (1:07:25; plan item #2). From public data DecisionPro can show now: (1) RAND's Kentucky commercial price as % of Medicare: 230.5% overall in 2022, 38th of 50 states (13th lowest), below the 252.8% state median, with inpatient, outpatient and professional splits and peers (Indiana 300.0%). (2) The same ratio for 74 of 86 Kentucky hospitals in RAND (2020-2022), median 235%, range 108%-422%, with claim counts. (3) Kentucky's Medicaid directed-payment design: HRIP lifts MCO hospital payments to 100% of the average commercial rate in CY 2026 (from 45% IP / 44% OP base). (4) A modeled bridge that puts Kentucky's Medicaid hospital payment level in % of Medicare terms (about 233% inpatient, 268% outpatient after directed payments), labeled Estimate. (5) Hospital finances alongside prices: margins, Medicaid revenue share, cash, Schedule H community benefit. What needs the Kentucky APCD or claims under a DUA: commercial prices by service line and payer for every hospital and for recent years; the fully insured market (RAND is mostly self-insured employer claims and does not use a Kentucky APCD); any validation of hospital MRF or payer TiC postings (Indiana's 21% match shows why they cannot be published unvalidated); per-hospital Medicaid payment as % of each hospital's own Medicare rate (needs DMS MCO encounters repriced through IPPS/OPPS); and standard bundles (#24). Hospital MRF samples for a shoppable basket are feasible from public files but were not completed in this pass (see unresolved).

CAVEATS FOR THE UI. Cash and days-cash figures are hospital-unit cost-report balances; system members show near-zero or negative cash because the system holds it, and a few flagship CCNs carry system investments (for example 180001, 180045 and 181311, each showing 2,900+ days). The days-cash headline uses only the 23 hospitals with no CMS-reported multi-hospital parent; 98 days is their median. A few small hospitals report values that look like filing errors (181325 Medicaid revenue above net patient revenue, set to null; 181309 and 181325 very high Title XIX day shares). Schedule H rows are by filing organization (EIN), not hospital; Appalachian Regional Healthcare's return covers West Virginia hospitals too, and multi-state systems that file outside Kentucky (CommonSpirit, Bon Secours Mercy, AdventHealth parent, LifePoint and HCA, which are for-profit) are absent; government hospitals (e.g., University of Kentucky, Murray-Calloway, Taylor) do not file Schedule H. Jennie Stuart reports net community benefit of $0 (offsetting revenue equal to expense) as filed. The HRIP % of Medicare figure is an estimate built from two sources on different bases; display it with the Estimate label and the comparability text.

SOURCE ACCESS. rand.org returned HTTP 403 to automated requests; the RAND annex was taken from the Internet Archive capture of the same rand.org file, and the report text from a copy hosted by the Vermont Legislature. ProPublica per-filing XML is behind a security check, so Schedule H was read from IRS TEOS XML (some 2025 batch zips use Deflate64, expanded with 7-Zip). No accounts, keys or terms acceptances were used. County for CCNs 180002, 180040, 180141 and 181331 (blank in the cost-report extract) and the McCracken spelling come from CMS Hospital General Information (data.cms.gov xubh-q36u, retrieved 2026-10-28); facility and organization names normalized for acronyms (ARH, UofL, TJ, CCMH, EMHFL) and Mc- prefixes.
